title: Federal inmate convicted of soliciting murder of prison officials in Texas
text:
Federal inmate convicted of soliciting murder of prison officials in Texas
A 39-year-old man with ties to New Jersey was convicted on Aug. 25 of soliciting the murder of multiple federal law enforcement officers while incarcerated at the Three Rivers Federal Correctional Institution in Corpus Christi, Texas.
A jury found Aramis Stuckman guilty on all eight counts after deliberating for about one hour following a two-day trial. According to evidence presented, Stuckman wrote three letters in October 2024 seeking the assault, torture, and murder of several officers in exchange for up to $50,000. The jury heard that he passed these letters to three separate guards and threatened one guard by warning he would be the next victim if he reported the letter to authorities.
The defense argued that Stuckman did not write the letters himself or have resources to carry out his solicitations. The jury rejected these claims and delivered a guilty verdict as charged. U.S. District Judge Nelva Gonzales-Ramos presided over the trial and scheduled sentencing for Dec. 1.
Stuckman faces up to 20 years in federal prison for each count of solicitation of murder, up to 10 years for each count of solicitation of assault and threatening a law enforcement officer, as well as a possible maximum fine of $250,000 per count. He remains in custody pending sentencing.
The investigation was conducted by the FBI with assistance from Special Investigative Services of the Bureau of Prisons. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Ashley Martin and Tyler Foster are prosecuting the case.
The U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas has offices across Houston, Galveston, Corpus Christi, Laredo, McAllen and Brownsville; employs more than 200 attorneys; covers 43 counties with a population exceeding nine million; focuses on prosecuting federal crimes and handling civil cases for the government; is part of the Department of Justice under the Attorney General; and has had leaders such as Alamdar Hamdani serving from 2022 to 2025—according to its official website and official history page.
